summary: Defines a profile for X.509 certificates used to validate AS paths in BGPsec. Router certificates are issued under the RPKI to routers in an AS. It also covers CRLs and certification requests, and updates RFC 6487.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8209 defines the identity card that a router needs to sign secured BGP route announcements. The card is an ordinary X.509 certificate with two special features: a key usage that marks it as a routing certificate, and an extension listing the network numbers the router is allowed to speak for. It is issued by the same chain of authorities that runs the RPKI.

questions: what is a bgpsec router certificate
how does rpki issue router certificates
subtitle: The certificate that lets a router prove it may sign route advertisements on behalf of its network.

tldr.problem: BGPsec lets every network along a route verify that the others authorised the advertisement, but it needs certificates that bind a public key to the networks a router may speak for.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles X.509 end-entity certificates for that purpose: a new extended key usage, id-kp-bgpsec-router, marks them, the AS Resources extension names the networks, and the RPKI certification authorities issue them under the same hierarchy as the rest of the RPKI.
tldr.outcome: A router can obtain a certificate that says exactly which autonomous systems it may sign for, and every relying party can check that binding against the RPKI hierarchy.

facts.label: Recommended common name
facts.value: ROUTER- followed by the ASN in hex

today: RFC 8209 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 6487 with the profile for BGPsec Router Certificates, the matching certificate request profile and the validation rules that relying parties apply to them.

sections.title: What a BGPsec Router Certificate Is For
sections.content:
The RFC defines a profile for X.509 end-entity certificates used in the context of certifying Autonomous System paths in the BGPsec protocol. These are called BGPsec Router Certificates. The holder of the private key associated with such a certificate is authorized to send secure route advertisements, BGPsec UPDATEs, on behalf of the autonomous systems named in the certificate.

A router holding the private key is authorized to send route advertisements to its peers identifying the router's AS number as the source. The key property BGPsec provides is that every autonomous system along the AS path can verify that the other autonomous systems along the path have authorised the advertisement of the given route to the next one along the path.

The document is a profile of RFC 6487, which is itself a profile of RFC 5280, so it updates RFC 6487. It establishes requirements imposed on a Resource Certificate used as a BGPsec Router Certificate, meaning it defines constraints on certificate fields and extensions for the certificate to be valid in this context. It also profiles the certification requests used to acquire such certificates, and specifies the relying party certificate path validation procedures for them.
sections.plainLanguage: BGPsec signs a route so that each network in the path can check that its neighbour really did agree to pass the traffic on. For that, each router needs a certificate saying which networks it is allowed to speak for. This RFC says what that certificate must look like.

sections.title: Where the Certificate Comes From
sections.content:
IANA issues a certification authority certificate to each Regional Internet Registry. The RIR in turn issues a CA certificate to an Internet Service Provider. The ISP in turn issues end-entity certificates to itself, to enable verification of signatures on RPKI signed objects, and the CA also generates certificate revocation lists. These CA and end-entity certificates are called Resource Certificates and are profiled in RFC 6487. RFC 6480 originally envisioned using Resource Certificates for manifests and Route Origin Authorizations.

This document defines another type of Resource Certificate. The issuance of BGPsec Router Certificates has minimal impact on RPKI certification authorities, because the RPKI CA certificate and CRL profile remain unchanged, and the algorithms used to generate RPKI CA certificates and the CRLs needed to check the validity of the certificates remain as specified in RFC 7935. The only impact is that RPKI CAs need to be able to process a profiled certificate request signed with the algorithms found in RFC 8208.

BGPsec Router Certificates are used only to verify the signature on a BGPsec certificate request, which only CAs process, and the signature on a BGPsec UPDATE message, which only BGPsec routers process. They are not used to process manifests and ROAs, or to verify signatures on certificates or CRLs.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate comes from the same chain that issues the rest of the RPKI certificates: IANA at the top, then a regional registry, then the network operator. Nothing else in the RPKI changes, apart from the authorities having to handle a slightly different request format.

sections.title: The Certificate Fields
sections.content:
A BGPsec Router Certificate is consistent with the RFC 6487 profile as modified by this document, so it is a valid X.509 public key certificate. This section lists only the differences from RFC 6487.

The subject is recommended to carry the literal string 'ROUTER-' followed by the 32-bit ASN, encoded as eight hexadecimal digits, with the serial number attribute holding the 32-bit BGP Identifier, the router ID, also as eight hexadecimal digits. When a certificate is issued to more than one router, so that the private key is shared, the choice of router ID is at the discretion of the issuer. The subjectPublicKeyInfo field is as specified in RFC 8208.

The Basic Constraints extension must not be present, because BGPsec speakers are end entities.

The Extended Key Usage extension must be included and must not be marked critical. This document defines one key purpose, id-kp-bgpsec-router, whose object identifier is { id-kp 30 }. A BGPsec router must require the extension to be present in a certificate it receives, and must reject a certificate that does not contain the BGPsec Router EKU even if it carries the anyExtendedKeyUsage object identifier. When several key purpose values are included, the router need not recognise all of them as long as the required one is present.

The Subject Information Access and IP Resources extensions are not used and must be omitted. The AS Resources extension must be included, must contain one or more ASNs, and the 'inherit' element must not be specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate names the router and the networks it speaks for. It carries one new marker, the BGPsec Router key usage, which a router insists on seeing before it will trust the certificate. It must not claim to be a certificate authority, and it must not carry the extensions that point at other resources.

sections.title: Requesting and Validating the Certificate
sections.content:
The certificate request profile is the one in Section 6 of RFC 6487 with four differences. If the Basic Constraints extension is included, the CA must not honour the cA boolean if it is set to TRUE. If the Extended Key Usage extension is included, id-kp-bgpsec-router must be present and the CA must honour the request for it. If the Subject Information Access extension is included, the CA must not honour the request to include it. The SubjectPublicKeyInfo field and the algorithms used to sign the request are those of RFC 8208.

Validation follows the procedure in Section 7 of RFC 6487 as modified by five rules: the certificate must include the BGPsec Router EKU, must not include the Subject Information Access extension, must not include the IP Resources extension, must include the AS Resources extension, and must include the subjectPublicKeyInfo field described in RFC 8208. A relying party needs to support the algorithms of RFC 8208, used to validate BGPsec signatures, as well as those of RFC 7935, needed to validate signatures on BGPsec certificates, RPKI CA certificates and RPKI CRLs.

The design notes explain the resulting behaviour. Because certification authorities are required by the certificate policy to issue properly formed BGPsec Router Certificates regardless of what the request contains, a request to issue a CA certificate still results in an end-entity certificate; a request for the key usage values keyCertSign and cRLSign results in a certificate with neither of them; a request without the BGPsec Router EKU still results in a certificate that has it; and a request with the Subject Information Access extension results in a certificate without it. The same applies to the AS Resources extension, which is always present even though it is not in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: The request a router sends is only a suggestion. The authority issues the certificate it says is correct, adding the key usage and the list of networks if they are missing and removing the parts that do not belong. A router then checks the certificate against the same list of rules before using it.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The document permits an operator to include a list of ASNs in a BGPsec Router Certificate. In that case the certificate would become invalid if any one of the ASNs were removed from any superior CA certificate along the path to a trust anchor. Operators could avoid this possibility by issuing a separate BGPsec Router Certificate for each distinct ASN, so that the certificates for the ASNs that are retained in the superior CA certificate would remain valid.

Certificates are stored in the issuing CA's repository, where a repository following RFC 6481 must use the .cer filename extension for the certificate file. The private key associated with a router end-entity certificate may be used multiple times, to generate signatures in multiple instances of the BGPsec PATH attribute Signature Segments, so one certificate validates multiple signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: One practical choice is whether to list one network in a certificate or several. Listing several is more convenient, but if a higher authority later withdraws one of them, every certificate that listed it becomes invalid. Issuing one certificate per network avoids that coupling.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6487 apply.

A BGPsec Router Certificate will fail RPKI validation as defined in RFC 6487, because the cryptographic algorithms used are different. A relying party therefore needs to identify the EKU to determine the appropriate validation constraint.

The certificate is an extension of the RPKI to encompass routers, a building block of BGPsec used to validate signatures on BGPsec signature segment origination of signed path segments. Its essential security function is the secure binding of one or more ASNs to a public key, consistent with the RPKI allocation and assignment hierarchy.

Hash functions from RFC 8208 are used to generate the two key identifier extensions, the Subject Key Identifier and the Issuer Key Identifier. Collision resistance is not a required property of one-way hash functions when used to generate key identifiers, but hash collisions are unlikely and possible. If one is detected an operator should be alerted: a Subject Key Identifier collision might cause the incorrect certificate to be selected from the cache, resulting in a failed signature validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate exists to bind a public key to a set of network numbers in a way that matches who was allowed to allocate those numbers in the first place. Because it uses different algorithms from ordinary RPKI certificates, a relying party has to look at the key usage to know which validation rules to apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC makes use of two object identifiers in the SMI registry for PKIX. One is for the ASN.1 module in Appendix A and comes from the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry, with the name id-mod-bgpsec-eku. The other is for the BGPsec Router EKU defined in Section 3.1.3.2 and Appendix A and comes from the SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose registry, with the name id-kp-bgpsec-router. These object identifiers were assigned before management of the PKIX arc was handed to IANA, and the references in those registries have been updated to point to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are registered: one for the module that defines the key usage, and one for the key usage itself, whose value is 30 under the standard list of key purposes.
